title: Scientists Turn Old Plastic Bottles Into Cookies You Can Eat
summary:
What if your empty water bottle could become a cookie? That sounds like magic, but scientists are actually working on it. Researchers at Southern Illinois University Carbondale have found a way to turn plastic waste into food.

Here's how it works. First, they take plastic bottles and old corn stalks. They use hot water and oxygen to break these materials into tiny pieces. Then they feed those pieces to yeast. Yeast is a tiny living thing, like the kind that makes bread rise. But these yeasts have been specially trained, like tiny chefs. They eat the plastic pieces and turn them into proteins, vitamins, and flavors.

Then the scientists mix those ingredients with fiber, starch, and something sweet. They put the mixture into a 3D printer, which builds the food layer by layer. The result? Little cookies called µBites. That's pronounced "microbites."

The idea started with NASA. NASA wanted to find ways to feed astronauts on long space trips, where no grocery store is nearby. But it could also help people on Earth after disasters, when food is hard to find.

One researcher, Lahiru Jayakody, said, "Microbes are very clever. So, we are using their traits to solve the problems we created." The cookies are not ready for taste tests yet. Scientists are still waiting for permission. But someday, your trash could be your snack!
why_it_matters: This shows how science can turn trash into something useful, and the same problem-solving you practice at school could someday help feed astronauts or families after a storm.

background_read: Every year the world throws away hundreds of millions of tons of plastic, and a lot of it ends up in rivers and oceans where it can hurt animals.

NASA (the U.S. space agency that sends people into space) has studied for years how to feed astronauts on long trips — the International Space Station even has a small garden where astronauts grow lettuce.
Scientists are also testing 3D-printed food, which is made by a machine that stacks soft food layer by layer instead of building with plastic or metal.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers at Southern Illinois University Carbondale, plus NASA, which wanted food for long space trips.
WHAT: Scientists turn plastic bottles and old corn stalks into proteins, vitamins, and flavors, then 3D print little cookies called µBites.
WHERE: In a lab at Southern Illinois University Carbondale in the United States.
WHY: To feed astronauts far from any grocery store, and to help people on Earth after disasters when food is hard to find.

perspectives.description: They see plastic waste as a free ingredient and believe clever microbes could someday feed astronauts and disaster survivors.
Some people may feel uneasy about eating something that started as a plastic bottle, and want lots of safety tests before taking a bite.
They like that trash is being reused, but point out that making less plastic in the first place would be even better for the planet.
